structured.observed_behavior: The reproduced employment-exit-probability series X_t (sep.dat, Figure 1 bottom panel) declines secularly from its early-1980s peak. In the shipped 1951-2005 series it peaks at ~0.049 (1981Q4), with 1980-1983 averaging 0.0443, falling steadily to ~0.029 by 2002-2005 (slope -0.00069/yr, a ~0.017 absolute / ~35% drop). The extended 1948-2010 series continues the decline to ~0.023 by 2006-2010. The three recession-associated unemployment spikes appear only as modest bumps against this downtrend: 1990-91 mean 0.037 (max 0.039), 2001 mean 0.032 (max 0.033), and the 2008-09 episode max ~0.027 — none reverses or sustains an increase above the prevailing trend.
structured.claim_paraphrase: The employment exit probability X_t has declined secularly since the early 1980s to the mid-2000s, and the three recessions (1990-91, 2001, 2008-09) produced only modest bumps rather than large sustained increases.

rationale: The reproduced X_t series produced by the step-2 two-state construction (output/two_state/sep.dat, the Figure 1 bottom-panel series) shows an unmistakable secular decline: annual means fall from ~0.044 in the early 1980s (peak 0.04899 at 1981.75) to ~0.029 by 2003-2004, with a fitted linear slope of -0.00069/yr over 1980-2005 (1980-1983 mean 0.04425 vs 2002-2005 mean 0.02898). The recession spikes appear only as small bumps embedded in the downtrend: 1990-91 mean 0.03719 (max 0.03922) and 2001 mean 0.03159 (max 0.033). The extended 1948-2010 reconstruction (output/two_state_1948_2010/sep.dat) continues the fall to ~0.023 by 2006-2010 and shows the 2008-09 episode peaking at only ~0.027 — again a modest bump, not a large sustained increase. This directly matches the claim's described behavior. The only recorded fix (fix_severity.json) is a benign opt-in tail-splice to extend the sample past 2005M1 and does not touch the core exit-rate estimation, so it does not undermine the shipped-series result.
